notes:
I've put together notes on most verses. Romans 7:14–25 is where the traditions really disagree, so it gets the most space. There are gaps. I ran out of searches before reaching netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org or oca.org, and found no Pentecostal, Anglican or hyper-grace material, so those are missing. The Catholic and Orthodox notes come mostly from Augustine and from Protestant sites describing those views.

---

## The main debate: who is the "I" in 7:14–25?

- **The views.** Kent Hughes (quoted on Precept Austin) sees three main readings: a non-Christian Pharisee under the Law (this was the view of the Greek Fathers); a normal Christian (the view of Augustine, Luther, and Calvin); or a carnal Christian. He takes the second view because Paul switches to the present tense. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_714-25
- **Who holds which.** Precept Austin says most of the commentators it lists read it as a believer: MacArthur, Piper, Luther, Calvin, Owen, Hodge, Bruce, Cranfield and others. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_714-25
- **Early church and Wesley.** Steven Cole (bible.org) says the "unbeliever" view was held by the church fathers of the first three centuries. Augustine held it at first and later changed his mind. John Wesley and many in the Arminian camp hold to this view. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-39-who-wretched-man-romans-714-25-overview
- **Cole's own view.** He thinks Paul describes himself as a new believer. Paul had not yet grasped that he had died to the law, and had not yet learned to live by the Spirit. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-39-who-wretched-man-romans-714-25-overview

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1:**
- Guzik says Paul is now explaining Romans 6:14 ("not under law but under grace"). The "law" here means the Law of Moses, and also the wider law known through creation and conscience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley says Paul is speaking mainly to Jewish believers, trying to wean them off their fondness for the Mosaic law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm
- Ironside: the law rules a person until death ends its authority. Since believers died with Christ, they have died to the law as a rule of life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_71-3_commentary

**vv. 2–3:**
- Ironside: just as a husband's death frees his wife, death ends the believer's tie to the law. It is not the law that dies. It is our death with Christ, which leaves us free to be joined to the risen Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_71-3_commentary
- Newell warns that both halves of the chapter (vv. 1–6 and 7–25) are easily misunderstood. He also says the KJV obscures the argument by leaving out the opening word "Or". https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_71-3_commentary

**v. 4:**
- Guzik: believers are dead to the law both as a way of living and as a way to be right with God. That freedom is not for living to ourselves. It is so we can be "married" to Jesus and bear fruit for God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/

**v. 5:**
- Guzik: under the law we bore fruit for death, because the law stirred up sinful passions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley: "in the flesh" means our natural state before believing in Christ. The law was only the occasion that stirred up those sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm
- Precept Austin: being told not to do something excites the flesh. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_71-3_commentary

**v. 6:**
- Guzik: we are freed from the law as a means of justification or of sanctification. The point is to serve God better, out of love rather than fear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley: "the oldness of the letter" means the bare, literal, outward way we served before. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-romans/

**v. 7:**
- Guzik compares the law to an x-ray. It shows what is hidden, and you can't blame the x-ray for what it finds. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley thinks Paul switches to "I" here to play a part, not to describe himself: a man, first ignorant of the law, then under it and sincerely, but ineffectually, striving to serve God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-7.html
- Augustine says Paul picked "You shall not covet" as a command that covers all sin, because every sin comes from evil desire. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1502.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: through this commandment a person learns that evil desire itself is sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/romans-7.html

**v. 8:**
- Guzik: a warning like "Don't do that!" can become an invitation to sin because our hearts are rebellious. The fault is in us, not the commandment. He links this to Augustine's story of stealing pears. https://enduringword.com/the-sinfulness-of-sin/
- Wesley: "sin" means inbred corruption. The commandment forbade it but could not subdue it, so it only stirred it up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm

**v. 9:**
- Wesley: "alive apart from the law" means the law had not yet been pressed home to the heart. Paul thought he had life and virtue. When the commandment reached his heart, sin flared up and his strength died away. He saw himself dead in sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm
- An older commentary on StudyLight compares sin "reviving" to dust in a room, which only shows when sunlight is let in. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/7-11.html

**v. 10:**
- Wesley: God really did intend the commandment as a means to life. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-romans/
- Wayne Barber: it brought death because it showed Paul he could not obey in his own strength. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_76-13

**v. 11:**
- Guzik: sin works by deceiving. It falsely promises satisfaction, offers excuses, and promises escape from punishment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley: while Paul expected life from the law, sin took him by surprise and killed his hopes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm

**v. 12:**
- Precept Austin: the law shows dirt like a mirror but cannot make you clean. Revealing and condemning sin does not make the law evil. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_710-131
- Guzik: the problem is in us, not in the law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/

**v. 13:**
- Guzik: sin becomes "utterly sinful" in two ways. It is shown up against the law, and the law provokes it. If sin can use something as good as the law, that shows how evil sin is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley: sin carried on in spite of the commandment, which made its guilt much worse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm

**v. 14:**
- Guzik: "carnal" means "of the flesh". A spiritual law cannot help a fleshly man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley: "sold under sin" means totally enslaved, like a slave bought with money. He reads vv. 7–25 as the whole journey of a person moving from the "legal" state to the gospel state. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-romans/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: a believer at the start of the new life is still "carnal". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/romans-7.html
- F. F. Bruce: Paul is a man living on two levels at once, the present age and the age to come. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_714-25

**vv. 15–16:**
- Precept Austin: Paul knows what is right and wants to do it. What he lacks is power, because the law gives none. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_714-25
- Wesley: "good" in v. 16 sums up all three words of v. 12 (holy, righteous, good). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm

**v. 17:**
- Vine and Godet: this is not an excuse for sin. Godet says Paul is showing how wretched his bondage is: he is not master even in his own house. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_717-20
- MacArthur: Paul's new inner self now disapproves of the sin that still clings to him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_717-20
- Denney (quoted by Wuest): to be saved from sin, a person must both own it and disown it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_717-20
- Wesley: sin acts like another person, a tyrant within. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm

**v. 18:**
- Precept Austin: Paul says nothing good is "in my flesh", not simply "in me", because in a believer the Holy Spirit lives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_717-20
- Wesley: "flesh" means the whole person as he is by nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm

**vv. 19–20:**
- Godet: this proves v. 14's "sold under sin". A stranger has forced his way into the house. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_717-20
- Newell: it was a terrible awakening for the forgiven Saul. He was now convicted not of sins but of indwelling sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_717-20

**v. 21:**
- Wesley: "law" here means an inner, compelling power that comes from corrupt nature. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/romans-7.html

**v. 22:**
- Guzik: Paul's real self is the one who delights in God's law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Precept Austin points out that the Holy Spirit is not mentioned in the passage. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_721-25

**v. 23:**
- Wesley: the "other law" is the inner pull of evil inclinations and bodily appetites. It takes him captive in spite of all his resistance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm

**v. 24:**
- Guzik: "wretched" carries the idea of being worn out by hard labour. Paul is exhausted from trying to please God by law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley: the struggle peaks here and the man begins to pray almost without meaning to. The deliverance has not happened yet. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm
- Gill: Paul groans under indwelling sin, not outward troubles, which still marks him as a regenerate man. Poole: the word describes someone worn out by constant fighting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/7-24.htm
- Spurgeon calls it the cry of a fainting warrior falling back into his Redeemer's arms. Brown: this is not a newly awakened sinner but a believer in agony. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/7-24.html

**v. 25:**
- Guzik: Paul admits the struggle goes on. Jesus works through us in the fight, not instead of us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-7/
- Wesley: "I myself" means the person Paul is playing, until he is delivered. That man is now utterly weary of his bondage, and upon the brink of liberty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/7.htm

---

## How the Protestant traditions differ (vv. 14–25)

- **Reformed:** A Monergism article says people from a Reformation background would probably call Romans 7 the best description of the Christian life in the Bible, a lifelong tension of being justified and sinful at once. https://www.monergism.com/christ-died-sins-christians-too
- **Reformed dissent:** Thomas Schreiner (TGC) disagrees. He says the passage describes total captivity to sin, which doesn't fit Romans 8:2. He reads the present tense as vivid description, not a time marker. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/romans-7-does-not-describe-your-christian-experience/
- **Baptist:** MacArthur says the struggle belongs to all believers, even the most mature. The brokenness shown is itself a mark of maturity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_714-25
- **Methodist/Wesleyan:** Wesley says applying this to himself or any true believer would contradict Romans 8:2. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-romans/ Vic Reasoner (Wesley Center) argues the man is a slave to sin: both unsanctified and unsaved. https://wesley.nnu.edu/arminianism/the-arminian-magazine/the-arminian-magazine-spring-1991/
- **Lutheran:** 1517 reads the passage through Luther's phrase *simul iustus et peccator*. The Christian is wholly a sinner and, at the same time, wholly righteous before God because of Christ. https://www.1517.org/articles/simultaneously-righteous-and-sinner-an-introduction
- **"Carnal" or "legalistic Christian" view** (Ironside, Chafer, Ryrie): this is a believer trying to become holy by keeping the law in his own strength. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_714-25 The KJV Bible Commentary says this need not be the normal Christian experience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_721-25

## Catholic and Orthodox
- **Augustine** says what remains in the baptised is "concupiscence", a lasting pull toward sin. It stays in "the body of this death" (v. 24), and believers are told not to obey it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/15071.htm He calls the "law in our members" (v. 23) the concupiscence of the flesh. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1507.htm
- **Catholic teaching**, as described on a Protestant site (Monergism): the Council of Trent taught that baptism removes original sin. The concupiscence left behind is not itself sin unless a person consents to it. The Reformers called it real sin. https://www.monergism.com/original-sin-concupiscence-and-total-depravity-rome-and-reformers
- **Catholic.com** says that in the 1999 Catholic–Lutheran Joint Declaration, both sides could accept *simul iustus et peccator* only in a limited sense, and differences remain. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/justification
- **Orthodox:** I found nothing on oca.org. The only mention is second-hand: Kent Hughes says the Greek Fathers held the "pre-Christian" view (see the debate section above).
